title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a matched sample N=300 (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms (model_calls_used = 300). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Crucially, because no validator-detected violations occurred and the shared_initial_candidate contract replayed identical initial outputs to both arms, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run: the experiment measures that inserting a verifier does not change compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract, but it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We compress provenance in the body and archive the preregistration, per-episode validator traces, execution manifest, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains but raises operational-security concerns: generated artifacts can introduce unauthorized reachability, break access controls, or otherwise enlarge attack surface. Prior surveys and system work therefore recommend execution oracles, constrained generation, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. We asked a focused operational question that is both preregisterable and empirically testable in an emulation setting: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To answer this we preregistered a paired N=300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1), implemented a deterministic Dockerized execution with two independent validators combined by logical OR, and executed the paired baseline vs guarded comparison under a shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls. Our three evidence-grounded contributions are: (1) a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation with archived per-episode validator traces and provider-call accounting; (2) a compact empirical finding that, under the chosen model, validators, and shared-generation contract, no forbidden-reachability was detected in either arm (n11=300), implying the repair path was not exercised; and (3) artifact-grounded design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier diversity, and repair budgeting) to guide follow-up stress tests that can exercise verifier-guided repair. We state this central limitation up front: because the shared_initial_candidate contract replayed the identical initial candidate to both arms and no validator-reported violations occurred, the study does not evaluate whether repair can rescue violating outputs.
sections.related_work: Three strands of prior work shaped this study. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness in code and infrastructure tasks by using execution feedback to guide repair (e.g., TerraFormer and verifier-feedback systems). Second, NetOps surveys and system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce risk. Third, emulation/testbed efforts show execution-based validation is practical for research-grade evaluation but emphasize external-validity gaps versus production devices and live traffic. Our study targets an evidence gap identified in this literature: a preregistered, paired, execution-validated experiment that quantifies whether verifier insertion reduces security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarially perturbed intents and with deterministic, archived accounting.
sections.methodology: Design, preregistration, and execution contract: We preregistered a paired binary confirmatory design (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) with N=300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha=0.05). Sampling, deduplication (exact and fuzzy), and sensitivity analyses were prespecified. To limit provider usage under the execution contract we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent a single initial LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms (model_calls_used = 300; maximum_model_calls allowed by the contract = 600). Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate; Guarded = same initial candidate validated by deterministic validators and allowed up to one repair LLM call if any validator flagged forbidden reachability (repair policy: max one repair per pair). All seeds, task manifests, and orchestration are archived in the evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome (compact): The run completed all planned episodes: planned = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed = 600, failed = 0; provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate: model_calls_used = 300. The primary contingency counts are n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate of ≈0.00994. Repair activity and verifier concordance: validators never reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, so no repair call was invoked (all validator_trace.repair_applied = false) and verifier_disagreement_rate = 0. Representative examples and machine-readable per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and accounting files are archived to permit verification (see short verification paragraph below). Table 1 (paired contingency) and Figure 1 (one-line summary) present the principal statistics compactly.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and causal constraints: The degenerate contingency (n11 = 300) arises from two coupled, archived design facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical initial outputs for both arms (reducing between-arm sampling variance), and (2) for the chosen LLM, task set, emulation, and validator set, none of the programmatic adversarial variants produced validator-detectable forbidden reachability. Under these conditions the paired McNemar test is uninformative about repair efficacy because no discordant pairs exist. Operational design lessons (artifact-grounded): (A) Generation semantics matter: using independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) increases the opportunity for discordant violating outputs; under our contract this would increase model_calls to ≈600 (execution manifest shows maximum_model_calls = 600 and model_calls_used = 300), so empirical power trades directly against provider cost. (B) Adversary potency matters: our programmatic one-variant-per-seed adversary did not trigger validator-detectable violations for this model–validator configuration; stronger, targeted adversaries are required to exercise repair paths. (C) Verifier strength and diversity matter: we combined an execution-style validator with a graph-based static reachability analyzer (logical OR); richer oracle families or production-grade oracles could expose different violations. Reproducibility and verification: the primary numeric outcomes (contingency, p-value, CI, Clopper–Pearson bound), provider-call summary (model_calls_used = 300), and the per-episode validator_trace fields (including repair_applied flags) are archived; a short verification paragraph below points to representative artifact filenames for spot-checking.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation with a declared LLM (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The run completed N=300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating initial candidates. Therefore the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this execution: the observed null paired difference should be read as evidence that, under the chosen primitives and shared-generation contract, verifier insertion does not change observed compliance when baseline is already compliant—not as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in more adversarial or independently generated scenarios. We release all preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable targeted follow-up stress tests (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, expanded repair budgets, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles) that can exercise the repair path and directly test the original confirmatory hypothesis. Short verification paragraph: The archived evidence bundle contains execution/execution_manifest.json (run interval and provider accounting), execution/model_configuration.json (declared model = gpt-5-mini), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (task seeds and protected_interfaces entries such as mgmt1), execution/responses/ (shared-initial and per-condition responses), execution/scoring/*.json (per-episode validator_trace with violation_count and repair_applied), and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11 = 300; see artifact hashes in the bundle).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl, and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
